contents.html: This report summarizes the discussion at the first “Cyber AI Profile Workshop” in April 2025 during which NIST sought feedback toward the development of a NIST Cybersecurity Framework Community Profile for AI. The Cyber AI Profile will provide guidelines for managing cybersecurity risks associated with AI systems and security capabilities. Discussions at the workshop focused on governance and operational challenges organizations face when adopting AI. It built on comments received in response to the February 2025 Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper.
contents.html_ja: 本報告書は、2025年4月に開催された最初の「Cyber AI Profile ワークショップ」での議論をまとめたものです。このワークショップで NIST は、AI 向けの NIST Cybersecurity Framework コミュニティプロファイルの策定に向けたフィードバックを求めました。Cyber AI Profile は、AI システムおよびセキュリティ能力に関連するサイバーセキュリティリスクを管理するためのガイドラインを提供します。ワークショップでの議論は、組織が AI を導入する際に直面するガバナンス上および運用上の課題に焦点を当てました。議論は、2025年2月の Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper に対して寄せられたコメントを土台としています。

contents.html: The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof-of-concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include developing management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of information other than national security-related information in federal information systems.

contents.html: On April 3, 2025, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence hosted a public workshop titled Cyber AI Profile Workshop. The event brought together stakeholders from government, industry, and academia to discuss questions in the Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] published on February 14, 2025, as well as comments received on the concept paper. This document provides a summary of the workshop’s discussions, including opening remarks, fireside chat, panels, and breakout sessions. These activities aimed to define Focus Areas, identify anticipated uses, and outline useful elements for the proposed Cyber Artificial Intelligence (AI) Profile. By incorporating insights from participants across various organizations, the workshop established a collaborative foundation for addressing AI-specific cybersecurity challenges while enabling organizations to harness AI’s transformative potential.
contents.html_ja: 2025年4月3日、国立標準技術研究所（NIST）の国立サイバーセキュリティ卓越センターは、Cyber AI Profile Workshop と題する公開ワークショップを開催しました。このイベントには、政府、産業界、学術界の関係者が集まり、2025年2月14日に公開された Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] に含まれる問いと、そのコンセプトペーパーに寄せられたコメントについて議論しました。本書は、開会の挨拶、ファイヤーサイドチャット、パネル、ブレイクアウトセッションを含む、ワークショップでの議論の概要を示します。これらの活動は、提案されている Cyber Artificial Intelligence（AI）Profile のフォーカスエリアを定義し、想定される用途を特定し、有用な要素の概要を示すことを目的としていました。さまざまな組織の参加者の知見を取り入れることで、ワークショップは、AI 固有のサイバーセキュリティ課題に取り組むための協力的な基盤を築くとともに、組織が AI の変革的な可能性を活用できるようにしました。

contents.html: Recent advances in AI technologies bring great opportunities to organizations, but also new and modified risks and impacts that need to be managed in the domain of cybersecurity. NIST is evaluating how to use existing frameworks, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0) [2], to assist organizations as they face these new or expanded risks. Feedback from the cybersecurity community strongly suggests that developing guidelines based on CSF 2.0 to address AI-related cybersecurity risks would be valuable.
contents.html_ja: AI 技術の最近の進歩は、組織に大きな機会をもたらしますが、サイバーセキュリティの領域で管理する必要のある、新しい、または変化したリスクと影響ももたらします。NIST は、組織がこれらの新しい、または拡大したリスクに直面する際に役立つよう、NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0（CSF 2.0）[2] などの既存のフレームワークをどのように使えるかを評価しています。サイバーセキュリティコミュニティからのフィードバックは、AI 関連のサイバーセキュリティリスクに対処するために CSF 2.0 に基づくガイドラインを策定することには価値があると強く示唆しています。

contents.html: Organizations vary in whether and how they use AI in their operations. Some organizations may not yet be using AI. Some may be using cybersecurity solutions enabled with machine learning (ML) technology for pattern detection and planning, but have not yet adopted newer, transformational AI capabilities, such as Generative AI. Regardless of where organizations are on their AI journey, they need risk management approaches that account for the realities of advancements in the use of AI to position them to defend against AI-enabled cyberattacks from adversaries and to leverage AI-enabled cyber defense capabilities. To address these emerging risks and opportunities, particularly in a rapidly evolving field, NIST is developing the Cyber AI Profile to identify how organizations can leverage and adapt the CSF 2.0 [2] to manage AI-related risks effectively [1]. The Cyber AI Profile will seek to help organizations integrate AI-specific considerations into existing cybersecurity programs by:
contents.html_ja: 組織が業務で AI を使用しているかどうか、またどのように使用しているかは、組織によって異なります。まだ AI を使用していない組織もあります。パターン検出と計画立案に機械学習（ML）技術を用いるサイバーセキュリティソリューションを使用しているものの、生成 AI などの新しい変革的な AI 能力はまだ採用していない組織もあります。組織が AI 活用のどの段階にあるかにかかわらず、AI の利用の進展という現実を考慮したリスク管理アプローチが必要です。それにより、敵対者による AI を活用したサイバー攻撃から防御し、AI を活用したサイバー防御能力を利用できるようになります。特に急速に進化している分野で、これらの新たなリスクと機会に対処するため、NIST は、組織が AI 関連リスクを効果的に管理できるよう、CSF 2.0 [2] をどのように活用し、適応させられるかを特定する Cyber AI Profile を策定しています [1]。Cyber AI Profile は、次のことによって、組織が AI 固有の検討事項を既存のサイバーセキュリティプログラムに統合できるよう支援することを目指しています。

contents.html: The workshop’s goal was to gather community feedback on the Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] to inform the direction and contents of the Cyber AI Profile. This concept paper outlined NIST’s initial observations and proposed approaches for addressing the intersection of AI and cybersecurity. Recognizing the transformative opportunities and risks introduced by AI, NIST sought input on whether existing frameworks, such as the CSF 2.0 [2] and the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) [3], could be adapted to address AI-specific challenges effectively.
contents.html_ja: ワークショップの目標は、Cyber AI Profile の方向性と内容を方向づけるため、Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] に関するコミュニティのフィードバックを集めることでした。このコンセプトペーパーは、AI とサイバーセキュリティの交差領域に対処するための NIST の初期の所見と提案するアプローチを概説しています。AI がもたらす変革的な機会とリスクを認識して、NIST は、CSF 2.0 [2] や Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework（AI RMF）[3] などの既存のフレームワークを、AI 固有の課題に効果的に対処するために適応させられるかどうかについて意見を求めました。

contents.html: This workshop was the first workshop, representing an early step in engaging stakeholders to define the scope of the Cyber AI Profile. The workshop explored the scope, focus areas, and practical applications of the Cyber AI Profile, with a focus on securing AI system components that leverage AI for cyber defense and thwarting AI-enabled cyber attacks. By engaging stakeholders across sectors, NIST aimed to ensure the development of meaningful guidelines that support organizations in managing AI-related cybersecurity risks while capitalizing on AI’s capabilities. Public feedback on the Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] informed the agenda and planned discussions for the Cyber AI Profile Workshop.
contents.html_ja: このワークショップは最初のワークショップであり、Cyber AI Profile の範囲を定義するために関係者の参加を促す初期の一歩でした。ワークショップでは、Cyber AI Profile の範囲、フォーカスエリア、実用的な応用を探りました。その際、サイバー防御に AI を活用する AI システムコンポーネントの保護と、AI を活用したサイバー攻撃の阻止に重点が置かれました。NIST は、さまざまな分野の関係者に参加してもらうことで、AI の能力を活用しつつ、組織が AI 関連のサイバーセキュリティリスクを管理するのを支援する、有意義なガイドラインの策定を確実にすることを目指しました。Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] に対する一般からのフィードバックが、Cyber AI Profile ワークショップの議事次第と予定された議論に反映されました。

contents.html: Jim St. Pierre, Deputy Director of NIST’s ITL, welcomed attendees to the NCCoE and expressed gratitude for their collaboration. He provided an overview of NIST’s mission to promote innovation and industrial competitiveness through measurement science, standards, and technology. Highlighting NIST’s non-regulatory status, he emphasized NIST’s ability to foster close industry collaboration without regulatory constraints. He also introduced ITL’s research areas, including cybersecurity, quantum computing, AI, and biometrics, and emphasized the importance of securing AI systems to align with NIST’s mission. Mr. St. Pierre concluded by thanking attendees for their input to help shape NIST’s outputs.

Ms. Pascoe encouraged active participation in the workshop, stressing the importance of community input in developing impactful guidelines.

contents.html: Katerina Megas, Program Manager for NIST’s Cybersecurity, Privacy, and AI Programs, provided an overview of the program, examples of ongoing and past work at NIST supporting the program’s mission, as well as the goals and structure of the workshop. A few examples of current NIST work within the AI space include the AI RMF, the Dioptra testbed, the Adversarial Machine Learning Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF), TrojAI, and the expansion of the NICE Framework (to include Competency Areas aligned to the AI RMF and CSF 2.0). She shared insights from preliminary stakeholder engagements, highlighting three key takeaways: the urgent need for AI-focused cybersecurity guidelines, the importance of leveraging existing frameworks, and the necessity of a common taxonomy to address cybersecurity challenges in AI.
contents.html_ja: NIST サイバーセキュリティ・プライバシー・AI プログラムのプログラムマネージャーである Katerina Megas 氏は、このプログラムの概要、プログラムの使命を支える NIST の進行中および過去の取り組みの例、ならびにワークショップの目標と構成を説明しました。AI 分野における NIST の現在の取り組みの例には、AI RMF、Dioptra テストベッド、Adversarial Machine Learning Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations、Secure Software Development Framework（SSDF）、TrojAI、NICE Framework の拡張（AI RMF および CSF 2.0 に整合するコンピテンシー領域を含める）があります。同氏は、予備的な関係者との対話から得られた知見を紹介し、3 つの主な収穫、すなわち、AI に焦点を当てたサイバーセキュリティガイドラインの緊急の必要性、既存のフレームワークを活用することの重要性、AI におけるサイバーセキュリティ上の課題に対処するための共通の分類体系の必要性を強調しました。

contents.html: The fireside chat featured NIST experts Steve Quinn and Martin Stanley, moderated by Dan Caprio, to discuss the interplay between the CSF 2.0 [2] and the AI RMF [3]. The discussion emphasized the need for executive-level governance and oversight to manage AI-related cybersecurity risks effectively. The NIST experts highlighted the importance of integrating AI into enterprise risk management strategies and aligning AI-specific risks with existing cybersecurity frameworks. They also explored the challenges of operationalizing AI risk management and the need for actionable guidelines to help organizations implement AI-enabled cybersecurity controls. Discussions also emphasized the importance of collaboration between AI and cybersecurity communities to address shared challenges and opportunities.
contents.html_ja: ファイヤーサイドチャットでは、NIST の専門家である Steve Quinn 氏と Martin Stanley 氏が、Dan Caprio 氏をモデレーターとして、CSF 2.0 [2] と AI RMF [3] の相互作用について議論しました。議論では、AI 関連のサイバーセキュリティリスクを効果的に管理するために、経営層レベルのガバナンスと監督が必要であることが強調されました。NIST の専門家は、AI をエンタープライズリスク管理戦略に統合し、AI 固有のリスクを既存のサイバーセキュリティフレームワークに整合させることの重要性を強調しました。また、AI リスク管理の運用化における課題と、組織が AI を活用したサイバーセキュリティ管理策を実装するのを支援する実行可能なガイドラインの必要性も探りました。議論ではさらに、共通の課題と機会に対処するために、AI コミュニティとサイバーセキュリティコミュニティの協力が重要であることが強調されました。

contents.html: The first panel of industry experts, moderated by Vicky Pillitteri, focused on identifying the scope, usage, gaps, and next steps for protecting AI systems from a cybersecurity perspective. Panelists highlighted that AI systems consist of multiple components, including data, models, applications, and infrastructure, each requiring tailored security measures. They noted that traditional cybersecurity concepts apply to AI systems, but there are differences in implementation that need to be addressed. Panelists also discussed the importance of understanding and applying current publications and references rather than reinventing the wheel or creating additional guidance, noting that duplicative guidance can be a burden for organizations when addressing threat modeling, supply chain security, and shared responsibility among stakeholders. Panelists highlighted the need for actionable implementation guidelines to address AI-specific risks, such as prompt injection and data poisoning, while leveraging existing cybersecurity principles, as well as the potential need for use case or industry-specific Profiles based on the Cyber AI Profile (after it is published). The discussion also stressed the importance of education and collaboration across teams to bridge knowledge gaps between AI researchers and cybersecurity professionals.
contents.html_ja: Vicky Pillitteri 氏がモデレーターを務めた、業界の専門家による最初のパネルは、サイバーセキュリティの観点から AI システムを保護するための範囲、使用法、ギャップ、今後のステップを特定することに焦点を当てました。パネリストは、AI システムはデータ、モデル、アプリケーション、インフラストラクチャを含む複数のコンポーネントで構成され、それぞれに個別対応のセキュリティ対策が必要であると強調しました。従来のサイバーセキュリティの概念は AI システムにも当てはまるものの、対処が必要な実装上の違いがあると指摘しました。パネリストはまた、車輪を再発明したり追加のガイダンスを作成したりするのではなく、現在の刊行物や参照資料を理解して適用することの重要性についても議論し、重複するガイダンスは、脅威モデリング、サプライチェーンセキュリティ、関係者間の責任共有に取り組む組織にとって負担となりうると指摘しました。パネリストは、プロンプトインジェクションやデータポイズニングなど、AI 固有のリスクに対処するために、既存のサイバーセキュリティの原則を活用しつつ、実行可能な実装ガイドラインが必要であることや、（公開後の）Cyber AI Profile に基づくユースケース別または業界別の Profile が必要になる可能性があることを強調しました。議論ではまた、AI 研究者とサイバーセキュリティ専門家の間の知識のギャップを埋めるために、教育とチーム間の協力が重要であることも強調されました。

contents.html: The second panel of industry experts, moderated by Martin Stanley, explored the use of AI in cybersecurity defense and the adversarial use of AI to augment cyberattacks. Panelists discussed how AI enhances cybersecurity tools by improving threat detection, incident response, and behavioral analysis. They highlighted the role of AI in enabling predictive path analysis and reducing alert fatigue for defenders. On the adversarial side, panelists noted that AI lowers the barrier for attackers, enabling faster and more scalable attacks, such as AI-crafted phishing campaigns and automated vulnerability exploitation. The discussion emphasized the need for defenders to leverage AI to match adversaries' speed and scale while addressing transparency, trust, and accountability in AI-enabled systems. Panelists called for red teaming, continuous risk evaluation, governance frameworks, and robust identity management to mitigate risks associated with adversarial machine learning and protecting AI systems after adoption. Panelists also acknowledged that there may be a need for additional regulation in this space to address any identified gaps.
contents.html_ja: Martin Stanley 氏がモデレーターを務めた業界専門家による 2 つ目のパネルでは、サイバーセキュリティ防御における AI の利用と、サイバー攻撃を増強するための攻撃者による AI の利用が検討されました。パネリストは、AI が脅威検知、インシデント対応、行動分析を改善することで、サイバーセキュリティツールをどのように強化するかを議論しました。また、AI が予測的なパス分析を可能にし、防御側のアラート疲れを軽減する役割を果たすことを強調しました。攻撃者側について、パネリストは、AI が攻撃者にとっての障壁を下げ、AI が作成したフィッシングキャンペーンや脆弱性の自動悪用など、より速く、より大規模な攻撃を可能にすると指摘しました。議論では、AI を活用したシステムにおける透明性、信頼、説明責任に対処しながら、防御側が攻撃者の速度と規模に対抗するために AI を活用する必要があることが強調されました。パネリストは、敵対的機械学習に関連するリスクを軽減し、導入後の AI システムを保護するため、レッドチーミング、継続的なリスク評価、ガバナンスフレームワーク、堅牢なアイデンティティ管理を求めました。パネリストはまた、特定されたギャップに対処するため、この分野で追加の規制が必要になる可能性があることも認めました。

contents.html: The Cyber AI Profile Workshop offered participants an opportunity to share feedback and insights with NIST throughout the day. These takeaways reflect ideas that resonated strongly across discussions and provide valuable feedback for NIST’s ongoing efforts for the Cyber AI Profile and other NIST programs. Participants emphasized the importance of integrating AI-specific risks into existing frameworks, adopting proactive defense strategies, and ensuring supply chain security. Transparency, accountability, and continuous monitoring were identified as critical for maintaining trust and system integrity. Participants also called for the Cyber AI Profile to be modular and adaptable, to include sector-specific Profiles, and to cover the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration to ensure the Profile’s relevance across diverse sectors and organizational sizes. Attendees requested that the Cyber AI Profile focus on risk management rather than compliance, providing actionable guidelines to help organizations navigate the evolving cybersecurity landscape shaped by AI technologies.
contents.html_ja: Cyber AI Profile ワークショップは、参加者が 1 日を通じて、フィードバックと知見を NIST と共有する機会となりました。これらの収穫は、議論全体で強く共感を得た考えを反映しており、Cyber AI Profile およびその他の NIST プログラムに対する NIST の継続的な取り組みに貴重なフィードバックを提供します。参加者は、AI 固有のリスクを既存のフレームワークに統合すること、事前対応型の防御戦略を採用すること、サプライチェーンセキュリティを確保することの重要性を強調しました。透明性、説明責任、継続的モニタリングは、信頼とシステムの完全性を維持するうえで重要であると特定されました。参加者はまた、Cyber AI Profile がモジュール式で適応可能であること、分野別の Profile を含むこと、そして Profile が多様な分野や組織規模で適切であり続けるように学際的な協力の重要性を扱うことを求めました。出席者は、Cyber AI Profile がコンプライアンスではなくリスク管理に焦点を当て、AI 技術によって形づくられる進化するサイバーセキュリティの状況を組織が進むのに役立つ実行可能なガイドラインを提供するよう要望しました。

contents.html: Multidisciplinary Collaboration and Education: AI use introduces considerations from multiple aspects of organizational operations, including legal, technical, procurement/acquisitions, and governance teams. Collaboration across these areas was highlighted as essential for addressing AI-related cybersecurity risks. Participants called for integrating perspectives through multidisciplinary teams to ensure a comprehensive enterprise view. They also discussed the need for education and cross-team collaboration to bridge the knowledge gaps between AI and cybersecurity experts.
contents.html_ja: 学際的な協力と教育: AI の利用は、法務、技術、調達・取得、ガバナンスのチームなど、組織運営のさまざまな側面からの考慮事項をもたらします。これらの領域にまたがる協力は、AI 関連のサイバーセキュリティリスクに対処するために不可欠であると強調されました。参加者は、包括的なエンタープライズの視点を確保するために、学際的なチームを通じて視点を統合することを求めました。また、AI の専門家とサイバーセキュリティの専門家の間の知識のギャップを埋めるために、教育とチーム間の協力が必要であることも議論しました。

contents.html: Dual-Use Nature of AI: AI's dual-use nature, both as a tool for enhancing defenses and as a means for adversaries to amplify attacks, presents both opportunities and risks. Cybersecurity considerations need to address these dual uses. AI can enhance cybersecurity tools, such as anomaly detection and incident response, but it can also enable adversaries to scale and automate attacks, including phishing, data poisoning, and model inversion. Proactive defense measures, such as automated red teaming and zero-trust principles, were identified as essential.
contents.html_ja: AI のデュアルユースの性質: AI は、防御を強化するツールであると同時に、攻撃者が攻撃を増幅する手段でもあるというデュアルユースの性質を持ち、機会とリスクの両方をもたらします。サイバーセキュリティに関する考慮事項は、これらのデュアルユースに対処する必要があります。AI は、異常検知やインシデント対応などのサイバーセキュリティツールを強化できますが、フィッシング、データポイズニング、モデル反転を含む攻撃の規模拡大と自動化を攻撃者に可能にすることもあります。自動化されたレッドチーミングやゼロトラストの原則などの事前対応型の防御策が不可欠であると特定されました。

contents.html: Effectiveness in Cyber-Defense: AI enhances cybersecurity efficiency, enabling faster data analysis and reduced reliance on third-party services. However, participants stressed the importance of measurable benchmarks to assess AI performance and mitigate challenges such as false positives and negatives, ensuring AI-driven cyber-defense capabilities perform as expected.
contents.html_ja: サイバー防御における有効性: AI はサイバーセキュリティの効率を高め、より速いデータ分析とサードパーティサービスへの依存の低減を可能にします。ただし、参加者は、AI の性能を評価し、誤検知・見逃しなどの課題を緩和して、AI によるサイバー防御能力が期待どおりに機能することを確保するために、測定可能なベンチマークが重要であることを強調しました。

contents.html: Supply Chain Security: The workshop underscored the importance of securing the AI supply chain, including the need to understand the origins of AI components (e.g., microservices, containers, libraries) and data, the new vulnerabilities they may introduce, and their potential impacts on cybersecurity. Discussions also covered open-source models, training and use of third-party models, understanding the impacts of model changes over time, and third-party dependencies (as well as the need for trust and provenance).
contents.html_ja: サプライチェーンセキュリティ: ワークショップでは、AI サプライチェーンの保護の重要性が強調されました。これには、AI コンポーネント（たとえば、マイクロサービス、コンテナ、ライブラリ）とデータの出所、それらがもたらしうる新たな脆弱性、サイバーセキュリティへの潜在的な影響を理解する必要性が含まれます。議論では、オープンソースモデル、サードパーティモデルの学習と使用、モデルの変更が時間とともに及ぼす影響の理解、サードパーティへの依存関係（および信頼と出所の必要性）も取り上げられました。

contents.html: Transparency: Participants called for greater transparency in AI systems used to support cybersecurity, including clear documentation of data provenance, model behavior, and decision-making processes. Concerns about the distribution of data leading to incorrect results were identified as areas requiring more focus to ensure trustworthiness in cybersecurity implementations.
contents.html_ja: 透明性: 参加者は、サイバーセキュリティを支援するために使われる AI システムにおいて、データの出所、モデルの挙動、意思決定プロセスの明確な文書化を含む、より高い透明性を求めました。データの分布が誤った結果につながることへの懸念は、サイバーセキュリティの実装における信頼性を確保するために、より注力が必要な領域として特定されました。

contents.html: Human-in-the-Loop: Participants stressed the importance of human-in-the-loop processes and training to ensure effective implementation and oversight of AI systems used for cybersecurity. Discussions highlighted challenges in understanding AI behavior, including the variability of responses and the difficulty in interpreting AI-driven decisions. Bridging knowledge gaps between AI researchers and cybersecurity professionals was identified as critical for enabling the two communities to work together to build and maintain trustworthy AI systems.
contents.html_ja: ヒューマン・イン・ザ・ループ: 参加者は、サイバーセキュリティに使われる AI システムの効果的な実装と監督を確保するために、ヒューマン・イン・ザ・ループのプロセスとトレーニングが重要であることを強調しました。議論では、応答のばらつきや AI による意思決定の解釈の難しさなど、AI の挙動を理解する際の課題が取り上げられました。AI 研究者とサイバーセキュリティ専門家の間の知識のギャップを埋めることは、両コミュニティが協力して信頼できる AI システムを構築し維持できるようにするうえで重要であると特定されました。

contents.html: Framework Integration: Participants emphasized the need for a shared understanding and common taxonomy between the AI and cybersecurity communities and noted the importance of integrating AI-specific risks into existing frameworks, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF), NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), NIST Privacy Framework, NIST Risk Management Framework (NIST RMF), and Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations. Suggestions included mapping to international standards, such as the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the anticipated ISO/IEC 27090, and leveraging other resources, such as MITRE ATLAS<sup>TM</sup>, for threat modeling. The need for sector-specific Community Profiles tailored to industries like healthcare, finance, and energy was also discussed.
contents.html_ja: フレームワークの統合: 参加者は、AI コミュニティとサイバーセキュリティコミュニティの間の共通理解と共通の分類体系の必要性を強調し、AI 固有のリスクを、NIST Cybersecurity Framework（CSF）、NIST AI Risk Management Framework（AI RMF）、NIST Privacy Framework、NIST Risk Management Framework（NIST RMF）、Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations などの既存のフレームワークに統合することの重要性を指摘しました。提案には、欧州連合の一般データ保護規則（GDPR）や予定されている ISO/IEC 27090 などの国際標準への対応付けや、脅威モデリングのための MITRE ATLAS<sup>TM</sup> などの他のリソースの活用が含まれました。医療、金融、エネルギーなどの業界に合わせた、分野別のコミュニティプロファイルの必要性も議論されました。

contents.html: Throughout the event, participants highlighted several important themes that extend beyond the immediate scope of the Cyber AI Profile. While these topics will not be directly addressed in the current iteration of the Profile, they offer valuable insights that may inform future initiatives for the AI Cybersecurity and Privacy Program and other NIST programs. By acknowledging these ideas, NIST reaffirms its commitment to adapting to the evolving needs of the community and exploring opportunities for continued engagement and development.
contents.html_ja: イベントを通じて、参加者は、Cyber AI Profile の直接の範囲を超えるいくつかの重要なテーマを強調しました。これらのトピックは Profile の現在の版では直接取り上げられませんが、AI サイバーセキュリティ・プライバシープログラムやその他の NIST プログラムの今後の取り組みに役立つ可能性のある貴重な知見を提供します。これらの考えを認めることで、NIST は、コミュニティの進化するニーズに適応し、継続的な関わりと開発の機会を探るという姿勢を改めて示します。

contents.html: Implementation Based on AI Maturity: Participants highlighted the need for the Cyber AI Profile to support diverse use cases and organizational contexts. This includes tailoring implementation guidance based on the maturity of AI adoption, such as developing models from scratch, fine-tuning existing models, or using third-party tools. By addressing these varying levels of maturity, the profile can help organizations apply security measures and governance strategies that align with their specific AI capabilities and risks.
contents.html_ja: AI の成熟度に基づく実装: 参加者は、Cyber AI Profile が多様なユースケースと組織の状況を支援する必要があることを強調しました。これには、モデルをゼロから開発する、既存のモデルをファインチューニングする、サードパーティのツールを使用するなど、AI 導入の成熟度に基づいて実装ガイダンスを調整することが含まれます。これらのさまざまな成熟度に対処することで、Profile は、組織が自らの AI 能力とリスクに合ったセキュリティ対策とガバナンス戦略を適用するのに役立てられます。

contents.html_ja: スケーラブルで適応可能なツール: AI 関連のサイバーセキュリティリスクを管理するための、スケーラブルで適応可能なツールの必要性が強調されました。参加者は、Profile をよりユーザーフレンドリーにし、多様な業界に適用できるようにするために、OLIR ベースの対応付けや LLM との統合など、Cyber AI Profile のインタラクティブでカスタマイズ可能な設計機能を提案しました。

contents.html: The workshop provided NIST with valuable feedback that validated the use of the three focus areas (Secure, Defend, and Thwart) and their definitions, and informed the Preliminary Draft of the Cyber AI Profile. The summer 2025 Community of Interest (COI) Working Sessions<sup>4</sup> followed up on several lines of discussion surfaced at this event. This stakeholder input is essential to the open, transparent process for developing the Cyber AI Profile. Each step of the process toward the Cyber AI Profile will build on the previous actions and information. Katerina Megas, Program Manager for NIST’s Cybersecurity, Privacy, and AI Programs, provided an overview of the program, examples of ongoing and past work at NIST supporting the program’s mission, as well as the goals and structure of the workshop. A few examples of current NIST work within the AI space include the AI RMF, the Dioptra testbed, the Adversarial Machine Learning Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF), TrojAI, and the expansion of the NICE Framework (to include Competency Areas aligned to the AI RMF and CSF 2.0). She shared insights from preliminary stakeholder engagements, highlighting three key takeaways: the urgent need for AI-focused cybersecurity guidelines, the importance of leveraging existing frameworks, and the necessity of a common taxonomy to address cybersecurity challenges in AI.

Harmonization: Identify existing guidance and understand how these emerging guidance documents can be used to develop a standard approach to cybersecurity and AI risk management. Suggestions included mappings to international standards, such as the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the anticipated ISO/IEC 27090, and leveraging tools like MITRE ATLASTM for threat modeling.

This session used the Functions and Categories of the CSF Core to begin identifying the top threats and unique considerations for the three Cyber AI Profile Focus Areas outlined in the concept paper. Participants emphasized the need to integrate AI-specific risks into existing frameworks and to provide actionable guidelines for organizations; they indicated they like the idea of treating the three Focus Areas separately to address their distinct challenges while recognizing areas of overlap, such as governance and monitoring. The table below provides an overview of themes that arose for each Focus Area by CSF Function and reflects cross-cutting themes across all three Focus Areas.3

Dual-Use Nature of AI: AI's dual-use nature, both as a tool for enhancing defenses and as a means for adversaries to amplify attacks, presents both opportunities and risks. Cybersecurity considerations need to address these dual uses. AI can enhance cybersecurity tools, such as anomaly detection and incident response, but it can also enable adversaries to scale and automate attacks, including phishing, data poisoning, and model inversion. Proactive defense measures, such as automated red teaming and zero-trust principles, were identified as essential.

Framework Integration: Participants emphasized the need for a shared understanding and common taxonomy between the AI and cybersecurity communities and noted the importance of integrating AI-specific risks into existing frameworks, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF), NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), NIST Privacy Framework, NIST Risk Management Framework (NIST RMF), and Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations. Suggestions included mapping to international standards, such as the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the anticipated ISO/IEC 27090, and leveraging other resources, such as MITRE ATLASTM, for threat modeling. The need for sector-specific Community Profiles tailored to industries like healthcare, finance, and energy was also discussed.

Implementation Based on AI Maturity: Participants highlighted the need for the Cyber AI Profile to support diverse use cases and organizational contexts. This includes tailoring implementation guidance based on the maturity of AI adoption, such as developing models from scratch, fine-tuning existing models, or using third-party tools.
By addressing these varying levels of maturity, the profile can help organizations apply security measures and governance strategies that align with their specific AI capabilities and risks.

The workshop provided NIST with valuable feedback that validated the use of the three focus areas (Secure, Defend, and Thwart) and their definitions, and informed the Preliminary Draft of the Cyber AI Profile. The summer 2025 Community of Interest (COI) Working Sessions4 followed up on several lines of discussion surfaced at this event. This stakeholder input is essential to the open, transparent process for developing the Cyber AI Profile. Each step of the process toward the Cyber AI Profile will build on the previous actions and information. This workshop was informed by comments received on the Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] and the themes gleaned from those responses. The insights from this workshop, as well as comments submitted on the Cyber AI Profile Concept Paper [1], informed the direction of the Cyber AI Profile Preliminary Draft.

Abstract

This report summarizes the discussion at the first “Cyber AI Profile Workshop” in April 2025 during which NIST sought feedback toward the development of a NIST Cybersecurity Framework Community Profile for AI. The Cyber AI Profile will provide guidelines for managing cybersecurity risks associated with AI systems and security capabilities. Discussions at the workshop focused on governance and operational challenges organizations face when adopting AI. 1. Introduction

On April 3, 2025, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence hosted a public workshop titled Cyber AI Profile Workshop. The event brought together stakeholders from government, industry, and academia to discuss questions in the Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] published on February 14, 2025, as well as comments received on the concept paper. This document provides a summary of the workshop’s discussions, including opening remarks, fireside chat, panels, and breakout sessions. These activities aimed to define Focus Areas, identify anticipated uses, and outline useful elements for the proposed Cyber Artificial Intelligence (AI) Profile. By incorporating insights from participants across various organizations, the workshop established a collaborative foundation for addressing AI-specific cybersecurity challenges while enabling organizations to harness AI’s transformative potential.
1.1. About the NIST Cyber AI Profile

Recent advances in AI technologies bring great opportunities to organizations, but also new and modified risks and impacts that need to be managed in the domain of cybersecurity. NIST is evaluating how to use existing frameworks, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0) [2], to assist organizations as they face these new or expanded risks. Feedback from the cybersecurity community strongly suggests that developing guidelines based on CSF 2.0 to address AI-related cybersecurity risks would be valuable.

Organizations vary in whether and how they use AI in their operations. Some organizations may not yet be using AI. Some may be using cybersecurity solutions enabled with machine learning (ML) technology for pattern detection and planning, but have not yet adopted newer, transformational AI capabilities, such as Generative AI. Regardless of where organizations are on their AI journey, they need risk management approaches that account for the realities of advancements in the use of AI to position them to defend against AI-enabled cyberattacks from adversaries and to leverage AI-enabled cyber defense capabilities. To address these emerging risks and opportunities, particularly in a rapidly evolving field, NIST is developing the Cyber AI Profile to identify how organizations can leverage and adapt the CSF 2.0 [2] to manage AI-related risks effectively [1]. The Cyber AI Profile will seek to help organizations integrate AI-specific considerations into existing cybersecurity programs by:
Establishing a shared understanding of AI-related cybersecurity priorities and considerations for any organization;
Fostering collaboration and communication across the AI and cybersecurity communities; and
Providing common AI cybersecurity target outcomes that organizations can use to support strategic planning efforts and cybersecurity assessments, based on the CSF Core.
1.2. Background for the Cyber AI Profile Workshop

The workshop’s goal was to gather community feedback on the Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] to inform the direction and contents of the Cyber AI Profile. This concept paper outlined NIST’s initial observations and proposed approaches for addressing the intersection of AI and cybersecurity. Recognizing the transformative opportunities and risks introduced by AI, NIST sought input on whether existing frameworks, such as the CSF 2.0 [2] and the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) [3], could be adapted to address AI-specific challenges effectively.

This workshop was the first workshop, representing an early step in engaging stakeholders to define the scope of the Cyber AI Profile. The workshop explored the scope, focus areas, and practical applications of the Cyber AI Profile, with a focus on securing AI system components that leverage AI for cyber defense and thwarting AI-enabled cyber attacks. By engaging stakeholders across sectors, NIST aimed to ensure the development of meaningful guidelines that support organizations in managing AI-related cybersecurity risks while capitalizing on AI’s capabilities. Public feedback on the Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [1] informed the agenda and planned discussions for the Cyber AI Profile Workshop.

NIST’s mission to foster innovation and competitiveness through standards and technology; and
The critical role of stakeholder input in shaping practical, impactful guidelines.

They also explored the challenges of operationalizing AI risk management and the need for actionable guidelines to help organizations implement AI-enabled cybersecurity controls. 2.3. Summary of Panel Sessions

The first panel of industry experts, moderated by Vicky Pillitteri, focused on identifying the scope, usage, gaps, and next steps for protecting AI systems from a cybersecurity perspective. Panelists highlighted that AI systems consist of multiple components, including data, models, applications, and infrastructure, each requiring tailored security measures. They noted that traditional cybersecurity concepts apply to AI systems, but there are differences in implementation that need to be addressed. Panelists also discussed the importance of understanding and applying current publications and references rather than reinventing the wheel or creating additional guidance, noting that duplicative guidance can be a burden for organizations when addressing threat modeling, supply chain security, and shared responsibility among stakeholders. Panelists highlighted the need for actionable implementation guidelines to address AI-specific risks, such as prompt injection and data poisoning, while leveraging existing cybersecurity principles, as well as the potential need for use case or industry-specific Profiles based on the Cyber AI Profile (after it is published). The discussion also stressed the importance of education and collaboration across teams to bridge knowledge gaps between AI researchers and cybersecurity professionals.

3. Key Takeaways

The Cyber AI Profile Workshop offered participants an opportunity to share feedback and insights with NIST throughout the day. These takeaways reflect ideas that resonated strongly across discussions and provide valuable feedback for NIST’s ongoing efforts for the Cyber AI Profile and other NIST programs. Participants emphasized the importance of integrating AI-specific risks into existing frameworks, adopting proactive defense strategies, and ensuring supply chain security. Transparency, accountability, and continuous monitoring were identified as critical for maintaining trust and system integrity. Participants also called for the Cyber AI Profile to be modular and adaptable, to include sector-specific Profiles, and to cover the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration to ensure the Profile’s relevance across diverse sectors and organizational sizes. Attendees requested that the Cyber AI Profile focus on risk management rather than compliance, providing actionable guidelines to help organizations navigate the evolving cybersecurity landscape shaped by AI technologies.

The summarized takeaways outlined below do not represent formal recommendations to NIST but rather serve as a foundation for future community engagement. These takeaways will inform NIST’s continued efforts to develop the Cyber AI Profile as a practical resource for organizations navigating AI-related risks and opportunities.

Enterprise Risk Management and Governance: Participants generally agreed that AI risk is organizational risk. As such, it is critical to integrate AI risk management into existing enterprise risk management practices and governance structures.

Multidisciplinary Collaboration and Education: AI use introduces considerations from multiple aspects of organizational operations, including legal, technical, procurement/acquisitions, and governance teams. Collaboration across these areas was highlighted as essential for addressing AI-related cybersecurity risks. Participants called for integrating perspectives through multidisciplinary teams to ensure a comprehensive enterprise view. They also discussed the need for education and cross-team collaboration to bridge the knowledge gaps between AI and cybersecurity experts.

Effectiveness in Cyber-Defense: AI enhances cybersecurity efficiency, enabling faster data analysis and reduced reliance on third-party services. However, participants stressed the importance of measurable benchmarks to assess AI performance and mitigate challenges such as false positives and negatives, ensuring AI-driven cyber-defense capabilities perform as expected.

Supply Chain Security: The workshop underscored the importance of securing the AI supply chain, including the need to understand the origins of AI components (e.g., microservices, containers, libraries) and data, the new vulnerabilities they may introduce, and their potential impacts on cybersecurity. Discussions also covered open-source models, training and use of third-party models, understanding the impacts of model changes over time, and third-party dependencies (as well as the need for trust and provenance).

Transparency: Participants called for greater transparency in AI systems used to support cybersecurity, including clear documentation of data provenance, model behavior, and decision-making processes. Concerns about the distribution of data leading to incorrect results were identified as areas requiring more focus to ensure trustworthiness in cybersecurity implementations.

Human-in-the-Loop: Participants stressed the importance of human-in-the-loop processes and training to ensure effective implementation and oversight of AI systems used for cybersecurity. Discussions highlighted challenges in understanding AI behavior, including the variability of responses and the difficulty in interpreting AI-driven decisions. Bridging knowledge gaps between AI researchers and cybersecurity professionals was identified as critical for enabling the two communities to work together to build and maintain trustworthy AI systems.

Implementation Guidance and Informative References: Multiple discussions stressed the need for guidance on implementing controls for AI systems and informative references to help organizations understand how to manage AI-related risks. See this related NIST effort: SP 800-53 Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAiS).

Data Governance: Data governance was identified as a critical topic, particularly for AI systems reliant on external or third-party data sources. Participants called for a separate Focus Area to address sensitive data and its use in AI systems, including privacy considerations. See this related NIST effort: Data Governance and Management Profile.

Additionally, there was significant emphasis on the need to supplement traditional cybersecurity measures with those tailored for AI. Examples of tailored approaches discussed during the workshop include:
Cryptographic signing for models.
Certification systems.
Use of AI Software Bill of Materials (AI SBOM) to enhance transparency and accountability in AI components.
Securing feedback loops, where model outputs are reused for further training or decision making, to prevent amplification of errors or adversarial manipulations.
Robust governance strategies to address risks, such as data poisoning and model manipulation.

Adaptive identity management and access control strategies and policies to address the growing and complex role of non-human identities, such as AI agents and applications, in organizational environments.

Incident response strategies and plans that distinguish attacks against AI models from traditional cybersecurity incidents and facilitate appropriate responses to attacks on AI systems (e.g., reverting to last known-good versions of models after model poisoning).
Data security throughout its lifecycle in AI systems (e.g., model inputs and outputs)
These takeaways provide a foundation for future community engagement.
3.1. Adjacent Considerations

Throughout the event, participants highlighted several important themes that extend beyond the immediate scope of the Cyber AI Profile. While these topics will not be directly addressed in the current iteration of the Profile, they offer valuable insights that may inform future initiatives for the AI Cybersecurity and Privacy Program and other NIST programs. By acknowledging these ideas, NIST reaffirms its commitment to adapting to the evolving needs of the community and exploring opportunities for continued engagement and development.

Tailored Support for Small and Medium Businesses (SMBs): Participants emphasized the need for the Cyber AI Profile to provide SMBs with tailored support, including simple acquisition questions and practical tools to address their unique challenges.

Sector-Specific Profiles: Discussions highlighted the desire for NIST to develop sector-specific Cyber AI Profiles and tailored incident response plans to address diverse use cases and ensure relevance across industries.

Scalable and Adaptable Tools: The need for scalable and adaptable tools to manage AI-related cybersecurity risks was emphasized. Participants suggested interactive and customizable design features for the Cyber AI Profile, such as OLIR-based mappings and LLM integration, to make the profile more user-friendly and applicable across diverse industries.
SP 800-53 rev 5 Crosswalk: Participants recommended leveraging NIST SP 800-53 controls to provide detailed, implementable security measures tailored to AI-specific risks.

AI Supply Chain Documentation: Participants advocated for the inclusion of an AI Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) to address supply chain risks associated with AI systems. This initiative would enhance transparency and accountability by identifying the provenance, authenticity, and security of AI components, including open-source models and third-party dependencies. Cryptographic signing and certification systems were suggested as additional measures to ensure the integrity of AI systems across the supply chain.

Workforce Development: Participants emphasized the need for workforce training and development to address AI-related cybersecurity risks and to prepare cybersecurity teams for the effects of adopting AI-enabled tools.
